medical.title: Youths with disruptive behavior and callous-unemotional traits need a broad range of treatments, study shows
medical.summary: Children and teens with disruptive behavior problems present major challenges to the people in their environment. But when parents seek mental health treatment for symptoms including aggression, defiance and serious rule-breaking, clinicians and researchers may not agree on the best approaches to take.

medical.title: One flash of red light could check health of bioprinted tissue and implants
medical.summary: Using 3D printers to create complex structures from biocompatible materials that can include living cells has the potential to revolutionize medicine. This process—3D bioprinting—has powered breakthroughs in tissue engineering, medical implants and reconstructive surgery and may ultimately allow for the creation of transplantable human organs.

medical.title: Weighted blankets shown to reduce anxiety in hospitalized patients
medical.summary: New research published in the American Journal of Critical Care found that patients reported significantly lower anxiety after a short treatment session with a 15-pound (6.8-kilogram) weighted blanket. The study is unique in its setting and patient population, with no previously published studies examining the blankets' use with acutely ill, hospitalized adults.

medical.title: Virtual reality-based digital defocus vision training may aid myopia in children
medical.summary: Virtual reality-based digital defocus vision training (DDVT) may be a promising adjunctive approach for pediatric myopia control, according to a study published online Aug. 27 in JAMA Ophthalmology.

medical.title: How the brain decides where to insulate its own wiring
medical.summary: In the complex circuitry of the brain, a fatty substance known as myelin plays a vital role in insulating neural wiring. It coats billions of axons in the brain and makes up about one-fifth of the organ in humans.

medical.title: Antifungal therapy shows potential for IBD patients with Candida overgrowth
medical.summary: A commonly used systemic antifungal medication may help reduce symptoms in a subset of patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) by restoring a healthier gut microbiome, according to a preliminary study by Weill Cornell Medicine investigators. The study, published in Nature Medicine, provides what is thought to be the first evidence that targeting intestinal fungal dysbiosis can reshape bacterial and fungal microbiome dynamics in patients with IBD and establishes a framework for mycobiome-guided precision therapies.

medical.title: Number of people with dementia living at home could double by 2040
medical.summary: A study conducted at the University of Helsinki indicates that the total number of people with dementia will grow significantly in the coming years, and the number of those living at home may even more than double after 2018.

medical.title: Online mental health care is here to stay: Here's how to navigate your options and find the right clinician
medical.summary: As a mental health nurse practitioner who sees patients both in person and via telehealth, I'm often struck by just how many of my patients would not have received any mental health treatment before the COVID-19 pandemic: the stay-at-home mother without any child care; the college student on a rural campus, many miles away from home or a clinic; the middle-aged man who is finally ready for help—but not ready to be seen by a neighbor in the waiting room.

medical.title: Gut bacteria linked to key brain chemicals in first-of-its-kind human study
medical.summary: The neuroactive potential of bacteria living in the human gut is associated with levels of key chemicals in the brain, according to a new study published in Molecular Psychiatry. The research team from the University of Surrey and the University of Roehampton found that microbial pathways involved in producing and breaking down neuroactive compounds were associated with levels of GABA and glutamate in specific regions of the human brain.

medical.title: Five ways the human body can sync up with other people
medical.summary: The myth that when women live together their menstrual cycles become synchronized has long persisted—despite research showing there's no evidence that this so-called McClintock effect exists. Any overlap that does happen is probably just down to chance.

medical.title: Experimental drug may disrupt immune circuits in pneumonia
medical.summary: A drug that blocks calcium release-activated calcium (CRAC) channels may help interrupt harmful immune cell interactions that drive severe viral pneumonia, according to a new study published in The Journal of Clinical Investigation. The findings provide new insight into how the experimental drug Auxora works and may inform future precision medicine approaches to treating pneumonia, said the study's senior author, G. R. Scott Budinger, MD, chief of Pulmonary and Critical Care in the Department of Medicine.

medical.title: Bacterial protein fragment drives tissue fibrosis, but antibody treatment can help
medical.summary: A bacterial protein fragment called corisin drives pulmonary fibrosis by infiltrating and disrupting cells' quality-control systems, researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and Mie University in Japan found in a new study. Meanwhile, blocking corisin with an antibody impeded the damage. The researchers published their findings in Nature Communications.

medical.title: Brain blood flow responds differently to pain and touch, mouse study finds
medical.summary: When the brain is stimulated, blood flow increases. For 30 years, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), one of the most powerful windows into the human brain, has operated on the basis of this connection. fMRI doesn't actually see neurons firing; it tracks changes in blood oxygenation.

medical.title: Car seat and seat belt misuse tied to more severe injuries in children
medical.summary: Despite decades of efforts to improve car seat and seat belt habits, more work needs to be done to protect children in motor vehicle crashes, according to new research from The Ohio State University College of Medicine.

medical.title: EFHD1 may turn fatty liver disease into injury, with inhibition reducing scarring by up to 60%
medical.summary: Obesity-related metabolic liver disease affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide, but only some of those livers develop scarring, become inflamed and eventually fail. University of Utah researchers have identified a protein, EFHD1, that appears to drive that transition by triggering an out-of-place antiviral immune response.

medical.title: Short mitochondrial protein may help protect the aging heart from inflammation and failure
medical.summary: Researchers from the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (NUS Medicine), have discovered that a relatively short protein may play an important role in protecting the aging heart. The protein, known as STMP1, is made up of 47 amino acids and helps maintain the internal structure of mitochondria, which are parts of cells that produce energy. The preclinical findings were published in Circulation.

medical.title: 'Social jet lag' could contribute to teenage anxiety
medical.summary: Early school start times and sleeping in on weekends could contribute to anxiety in teenagers, a new study found.

science.title: Study: Reservoir management system could save California $150 million every year
science.summary: A new study from the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes (CW3E) at Scripps Institution of Oceanography at UC San Diego finds that improved weather and water forecasts could help California gain more value from existing reservoirs and help meet a new water supply target.

science.title: First measurement of low-energy solar neutrinos scattering off electrons
science.summary: Every second, tens of billions of neutrinos produced by nuclear fusion in the sun pass through every square centimeter of Earth—and through our bodies—almost without interacting. Although they are among the most abundant particles emitted by the sun, their extremely weak interactions make detecting these elusive particles one of the greatest experimental challenges in particle physics. A number of specialized neutrino detectors are in operation around the world, exploiting the unique properties of neutrinos to investigate astrophysical phenomena.

science.title: Remote work offers flexibility, but at the cost of learning opportunities for young workers
science.summary: Six years after the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the shift to remote work, hybrid and remote arrangements have become an established part of the labor market. About one in five Canadians now works remotely some or all of the time.

science.title: New AI approaches to help understand complex biological data
science.summary: Researchers at Cardiff University have presented two studies at the 2026 International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026) that address fundamental challenges in modern AI: understanding the complex geometry and relationships within data and recognizing patterns that occur across very different scales.

science.title: New AI model maps the ion binding sites that control how proteins work
science.summary: Researchers at Constructor University and Constructor Labs have developed BiteNetI, a deep-learning model that locates the binding sites of 14 biologically important ion types directly in three-dimensional protein structures. The model needs only several seconds per structure and reaches two- to threefold higher accuracy than most existing predictors, including Google DeepMind's AlphaFold 3. The study, authored by Igor Kozlovskii and Petr Popov, has been published in the journal Communications Biology. The tool provides an open-access platform that could help accelerate drug discovery and the understanding of protein function.

science.title: Forest floor to treetops, cameras reveal Congo Basin's hidden wildlife
science.summary: The Democratic Republic of Congo's (DRC) tropical forests stretch across an extraordinary landscape of rivers, wetlands, savannas and towering trees. But in a forest this vast, biodiversity doesn't exist on a single plane. It climbs into the canopy. It moves between branches and vines, disappears into the understory and travels across the forest floor.

science.title: Ten-channel photonic interface links neutral-atom qubits in parallel
science.summary: A research group in Japan has demonstrated a world-record 10-channel multiplexed quantum photonic interface based on an integrated waveguide array, a key technology for optically interconnecting multiple quantum computers. The study is published in the journal Optica.

science.title: Non-police safety practitioners reduce crime
science.summary: Non-police community guardians can effectively reduce crime by building relationships in urban disorder hotspots, according to a study.

science.title: Geomagnetic superstorm shook GPS accuracy across the US—its timing may have averted agricultural losses
science.summary: On Nov. 11, 2025, Earth experienced a severe geomagnetic storm triggered by solar flares and coronal mass ejections from an active sunspot region. While this kind of storm brings beautiful auroras admired in many areas around the world, it can also cause ionospheric disturbances that disrupt radio waves and affect crucial technologies. A new study, published in Geophysical Research Letters, found that disruptions caused by this storm scrambled GPS signals in areas where such disruptions have never been reported.

science.title: Largest review finds formal ethics education improves students' moral reasoning
science.summary: How important is it that kids learn to tell right from wrong? Businessman and former university chancellor David Gonski recently called for ethics classes to be rolled out in all Australian schools to boost social cohesion.

science.title: Anti-influenza therapies that target the host
science.summary: A drug that targets the host rather than the virus could get around the problem of antiviral resistance. Every year, hundreds of thousands of people die of seasonal influenza caused by infection with influenza A and B viruses.

science.title: UK chalks up hottest summer on record for second year running
science.summary: Britain experienced its hottest summer on record for the second year in a row, the UK's national weather agency announced Tuesday, after weeks of successive heat waves and widespread drought conditions.

science.title: Experiment sees surprising result in search for dark matter
science.summary: For the better part of a century, people have been trying to understand dark matter. This invisible substance makes up roughly 85% of the mass in the universe but has never been directly detected. Determining exactly what it is remains one of the biggest questions about our world.

science.title: For a century, journalists have had a voluntary ethics code. Editors are giving it an AI-era reboot
science.summary: Walk into a corner of a newsroom somewhere and you can often find it affixed to a bulletin board, perhaps peeking out from behind the coffee pot: the Society of Professional Journalists's Code of Ethics. It's less than a thousand words, fitting neatly on a poster.

science.title: Trawling threatens vital carbon stores in Scotland's sea lochs
science.summary: New research from the University of St Andrews shows that disturbing seabed sediments through trawling could cause significant losses of carbon stored in Scotland's sea lochs. The study, published in Marine Environmental Research, shows that organic carbon stored in seabed sediments can be released into the surrounding seawater when disturbed. This carbon is then more likely to be broken down and ultimately returned to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, contributing to climate change.

science.title: Marmite lures discovery from lake depths
science.summary: Dr. Roe Stuart didn't find a taniwha in the unexplored depths of New Zealand's lakes—but they may have found a new species of fish.

science.title: Ultrafast snapshots reveal the first moments on the way from light to electricity
science.summary: Physicists at the University of Graz (Austria), in collaboration with colleagues from Marburg University and Forschungszentrum Jülich (Germany), have achieved a scientific breakthrough. For the first time, the generation of electrical energy from light has been filmed and described theoretically.

environment.title: Superb fairywrens disappearing in Australia’s capital: Conserving insects could help save them
environment.summary: If you sit in an Australian park or garden for long enough, chances are you might catch a flash of brilliant feathers out of the corner of your eye: the superb fairywren. With its bright blue and soft brown plumage, it was voted Australia’s “bird of the year” in 2021, “narrowly defeating the tawny frogmouth […]

environment.summary: Founder’s Briefs: An occasional series where Mongabay founder Rhett Ayers Butler shares analysis, perspectives and story summaries. environment.title: ‘You can’t protect what you don’t know:’ Interview with marine scientist Loyiso Dunga
environment.summary: CAPE TOWN — When scientist Loyiso Dunga began mapping the Great African Seaforest in 2016, he decided to go snorkeling. The South African section of the kelp forest stretches around 800 miles or 1,300 kilometers, straddling two coasts and two oceans. Dunga grew up in a coastal community, Nqabara, in South Africa’s Wild Coast. As […]

environment.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
environment.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

environment.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
environment.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

environment.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
environment.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

environment.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.

mix_items.title: Study: Reservoir management system could save California $150 million every year
mix_items.summary: A new study from the Center for Western Weather and Water Extremes (CW3E) at Scripps Institution of Oceanography at UC San Diego finds that improved weather and water forecasts could help California gain more value from existing reservoirs and help meet a new water supply target.

mix_items.title: First measurement of low-energy solar neutrinos scattering off electrons
mix_items.summary: Every second, tens of billions of neutrinos produced by nuclear fusion in the sun pass through every square centimeter of Earth—and through our bodies—almost without interacting. Although they are among the most abundant particles emitted by the sun, their extremely weak interactions make detecting these elusive particles one of the greatest experimental challenges in particle physics. A number of specialized neutrino detectors are in operation around the world, exploiting the unique properties of neutrinos to investigate astrophysical phenomena.

mix_items.title: Youths with disruptive behavior and callous-unemotional traits need a broad range of treatments, study shows
mix_items.summary: Children and teens with disruptive behavior problems present major challenges to the people in their environment. But when parents seek mental health treatment for symptoms including aggression, defiance and serious rule-breaking, clinicians and researchers may not agree on the best approaches to take.

mix_items.title: One flash of red light could check health of bioprinted tissue and implants
mix_items.summary: Using 3D printers to create complex structures from biocompatible materials that can include living cells has the potential to revolutionize medicine. This process—3D bioprinting—has powered breakthroughs in tissue engineering, medical implants and reconstructive surgery and may ultimately allow for the creation of transplantable human organs.

mix_items.title: Weighted blankets shown to reduce anxiety in hospitalized patients
mix_items.summary: New research published in the American Journal of Critical Care found that patients reported significantly lower anxiety after a short treatment session with a 15-pound (6.8-kilogram) weighted blanket. The study is unique in its setting and patient population, with no previously published studies examining the blankets' use with acutely ill, hospitalized adults.

mix_items.title: Remote work offers flexibility, but at the cost of learning opportunities for young workers
mix_items.summary: Six years after the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated the shift to remote work, hybrid and remote arrangements have become an established part of the labor market. About one in five Canadians now works remotely some or all of the time.

mix_items.title: New AI approaches to help understand complex biological data
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Cardiff University have presented two studies at the 2026 International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026) that address fundamental challenges in modern AI: understanding the complex geometry and relationships within data and recognizing patterns that occur across very different scales.

mix_items.title: Virtual reality-based digital defocus vision training may aid myopia in children
mix_items.summary: Virtual reality-based digital defocus vision training (DDVT) may be a promising adjunctive approach for pediatric myopia control, according to a study published online Aug. 27 in JAMA Ophthalmology.

mix_items.title: How the brain decides where to insulate its own wiring
mix_items.summary: In the complex circuitry of the brain, a fatty substance known as myelin plays a vital role in insulating neural wiring. It coats billions of axons in the brain and makes up about one-fifth of the organ in humans.

mix_items.title: Antifungal therapy shows potential for IBD patients with Candida overgrowth
mix_items.summary: A commonly used systemic antifungal medication may help reduce symptoms in a subset of patients with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) by restoring a healthier gut microbiome, according to a preliminary study by Weill Cornell Medicine investigators. The study, published in Nature Medicine, provides what is thought to be the first evidence that targeting intestinal fungal dysbiosis can reshape bacterial and fungal microbiome dynamics in patients with IBD and establishes a framework for mycobiome-guided precision therapies.

mix_items.title: Number of people with dementia living at home could double by 2040
mix_items.summary: A study conducted at the University of Helsinki indicates that the total number of people with dementia will grow significantly in the coming years, and the number of those living at home may even more than double after 2018.

mix_items.title: New AI model maps the ion binding sites that control how proteins work
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Constructor University and Constructor Labs have developed BiteNetI, a deep-learning model that locates the binding sites of 14 biologically important ion types directly in three-dimensional protein structures. The model needs only several seconds per structure and reaches two- to threefold higher accuracy than most existing predictors, including Google DeepMind's AlphaFold 3. The study, authored by Igor Kozlovskii and Petr Popov, has been published in the journal Communications Biology. The tool provides an open-access platform that could help accelerate drug discovery and the understanding of protein function.

mix_items.title: Online mental health care is here to stay: Here's how to navigate your options and find the right clinician
mix_items.summary: As a mental health nurse practitioner who sees patients both in person and via telehealth, I'm often struck by just how many of my patients would not have received any mental health treatment before the COVID-19 pandemic: the stay-at-home mother without any child care; the college student on a rural campus, many miles away from home or a clinic; the middle-aged man who is finally ready for help—but not ready to be seen by a neighbor in the waiting room.

mix_items.title: Forest floor to treetops, cameras reveal Congo Basin's hidden wildlife
mix_items.summary: The Democratic Republic of Congo's (DRC) tropical forests stretch across an extraordinary landscape of rivers, wetlands, savannas and towering trees. But in a forest this vast, biodiversity doesn't exist on a single plane. It climbs into the canopy. It moves between branches and vines, disappears into the understory and travels across the forest floor.

mix_items.title: Gut bacteria linked to key brain chemicals in first-of-its-kind human study
mix_items.summary: The neuroactive potential of bacteria living in the human gut is associated with levels of key chemicals in the brain, according to a new study published in Molecular Psychiatry. The research team from the University of Surrey and the University of Roehampton found that microbial pathways involved in producing and breaking down neuroactive compounds were associated with levels of GABA and glutamate in specific regions of the human brain.

mix_items.title: Five ways the human body can sync up with other people
mix_items.summary: The myth that when women live together their menstrual cycles become synchronized has long persisted—despite research showing there's no evidence that this so-called McClintock effect exists. Any overlap that does happen is probably just down to chance.

mix_items.title: Ten-channel photonic interface links neutral-atom qubits in parallel
mix_items.summary: A research group in Japan has demonstrated a world-record 10-channel multiplexed quantum photonic interface based on an integrated waveguide array, a key technology for optically interconnecting multiple quantum computers. The study is published in the journal Optica.

mix_items.title: Experimental drug may disrupt immune circuits in pneumonia
mix_items.summary: A drug that blocks calcium release-activated calcium (CRAC) channels may help interrupt harmful immune cell interactions that drive severe viral pneumonia, according to a new study published in The Journal of Clinical Investigation. The findings provide new insight into how the experimental drug Auxora works and may inform future precision medicine approaches to treating pneumonia, said the study's senior author, G. R. Scott Budinger, MD, chief of Pulmonary and Critical Care in the Department of Medicine.

mix_items.title: Non-police safety practitioners reduce crime
mix_items.summary: Non-police community guardians can effectively reduce crime by building relationships in urban disorder hotspots, according to a study.

mix_items.title: Bacterial protein fragment drives tissue fibrosis, but antibody treatment can help
mix_items.summary: A bacterial protein fragment called corisin drives pulmonary fibrosis by infiltrating and disrupting cells' quality-control systems, researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and Mie University in Japan found in a new study. Meanwhile, blocking corisin with an antibody impeded the damage. The researchers published their findings in Nature Communications.

mix_items.title: Geomagnetic superstorm shook GPS accuracy across the US—its timing may have averted agricultural losses
mix_items.summary: On Nov. 11, 2025, Earth experienced a severe geomagnetic storm triggered by solar flares and coronal mass ejections from an active sunspot region. While this kind of storm brings beautiful auroras admired in many areas around the world, it can also cause ionospheric disturbances that disrupt radio waves and affect crucial technologies. A new study, published in Geophysical Research Letters, found that disruptions caused by this storm scrambled GPS signals in areas where such disruptions have never been reported.

mix_items.title: Largest review finds formal ethics education improves students' moral reasoning
mix_items.summary: How important is it that kids learn to tell right from wrong? Businessman and former university chancellor David Gonski recently called for ethics classes to be rolled out in all Australian schools to boost social cohesion.

mix_items.title: Anti-influenza therapies that target the host
mix_items.summary: A drug that targets the host rather than the virus could get around the problem of antiviral resistance. Every year, hundreds of thousands of people die of seasonal influenza caused by infection with influenza A and B viruses.

mix_items.title: Brain blood flow responds differently to pain and touch, mouse study finds
mix_items.summary: When the brain is stimulated, blood flow increases. For 30 years, functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), one of the most powerful windows into the human brain, has operated on the basis of this connection. fMRI doesn't actually see neurons firing; it tracks changes in blood oxygenation.

mix_items.title: Car seat and seat belt misuse tied to more severe injuries in children
mix_items.summary: Despite decades of efforts to improve car seat and seat belt habits, more work needs to be done to protect children in motor vehicle crashes, according to new research from The Ohio State University College of Medicine.

mix_items.title: UK chalks up hottest summer on record for second year running
mix_items.summary: Britain experienced its hottest summer on record for the second year in a row, the UK's national weather agency announced Tuesday, after weeks of successive heat waves and widespread drought conditions.

mix_items.title: Experiment sees surprising result in search for dark matter
mix_items.summary: For the better part of a century, people have been trying to understand dark matter. This invisible substance makes up roughly 85% of the mass in the universe but has never been directly detected. Determining exactly what it is remains one of the biggest questions about our world.

mix_items.title: For a century, journalists have had a voluntary ethics code. Editors are giving it an AI-era reboot
mix_items.summary: Walk into a corner of a newsroom somewhere and you can often find it affixed to a bulletin board, perhaps peeking out from behind the coffee pot: the Society of Professional Journalists's Code of Ethics. It's less than a thousand words, fitting neatly on a poster.

mix_items.title: EFHD1 may turn fatty liver disease into injury, with inhibition reducing scarring by up to 60%
mix_items.summary: Obesity-related metabolic liver disease affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide, but only some of those livers develop scarring, become inflamed and eventually fail. University of Utah researchers have identified a protein, EFHD1, that appears to drive that transition by triggering an out-of-place antiviral immune response.

mix_items.title: Short mitochondrial protein may help protect the aging heart from inflammation and failure
mix_items.summary: Researchers from the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (NUS Medicine), have discovered that a relatively short protein may play an important role in protecting the aging heart. The protein, known as STMP1, is made up of 47 amino acids and helps maintain the internal structure of mitochondria, which are parts of cells that produce energy. The preclinical findings were published in Circulation.

mix_items.title: Trawling threatens vital carbon stores in Scotland's sea lochs
mix_items.summary: New research from the University of St Andrews shows that disturbing seabed sediments through trawling could cause significant losses of carbon stored in Scotland's sea lochs. The study, published in Marine Environmental Research, shows that organic carbon stored in seabed sediments can be released into the surrounding seawater when disturbed. This carbon is then more likely to be broken down and ultimately returned to the atmosphere as carbon dioxide, contributing to climate change.

mix_items.title: Marmite lures discovery from lake depths
mix_items.summary: Dr. Roe Stuart didn't find a taniwha in the unexplored depths of New Zealand's lakes—but they may have found a new species of fish.

mix_items.title: Ultrafast snapshots reveal the first moments on the way from light to electricity
mix_items.summary: Physicists at the University of Graz (Austria), in collaboration with colleagues from Marburg University and Forschungszentrum Jülich (Germany), have achieved a scientific breakthrough. For the first time, the generation of electrical energy from light has been filmed and described theoretically.

mix_items.title: 'Social jet lag' could contribute to teenage anxiety
mix_items.summary: Early school start times and sleeping in on weekends could contribute to anxiety in teenagers, a new study found.

mix_items.title: Gold miners breach a crucial refuge for rescued Sumatran orangutans
mix_items.summary: JANTHO, Indonesia — Illegal gold miners in Indonesia’s Aceh province have breached a crucial reintroduction forest for critically endangered Sumatran orangutans rescued from the illegal wildlife trade. “The result of our monitoring indicates that maybe dozens of excavators are suspected of operating in the Jantho forest area,” said Afifuddin, campaign and advocacy lead at the […]

mix_items.title: Superb fairywrens disappearing in Australia’s capital: Conserving insects could help save them
mix_items.summary: If you sit in an Australian park or garden for long enough, chances are you might catch a flash of brilliant feathers out of the corner of your eye: the superb fairywren. With its bright blue and soft brown plumage, it was voted Australia’s “bird of the year” in 2021, “narrowly defeating the tawny frogmouth […]

mix_items.summary: Founder’s Briefs: An occasional series where Mongabay founder Rhett Ayers Butler shares analysis, perspectives and story summaries. In the forests around Pemaluan in East Kalimantan, Indonesian Borneo, researchers led by Wendy Erb at the Cornell K. Lisa Yang Center for Conservation Bioacoustics in the U.S. have placed audio recorders on mountains, beside caves, and among […]

mix_items.title: ‘You can’t protect what you don’t know:’ Interview with marine scientist Loyiso Dunga
mix_items.summary: CAPE TOWN — When scientist Loyiso Dunga began mapping the Great African Seaforest in 2016, he decided to go snorkeling. The South African section of the kelp forest stretches around 800 miles or 1,300 kilometers, straddling two coasts and two oceans. Dunga grew up in a coastal community, Nqabara, in South Africa’s Wild Coast. As […]

mix_items.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals ancient waterproofing secrets
mix_items.summary: Scientists analyzing a 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck found that its hull was coated with pine tar and, in one area, a mixture of tar and beeswax. Pollen trapped in those ancient coatings acted like a geographic fingerprint, revealing the landscapes surrounding the ship when repairs were made.

mix_items.title: A lost mega-cliff may explain the Grand Canyon’s missing billion years
mix_items.summary: A colossal cliff system created as the supercontinent Rodinia broke apart may have exposed the heart of the Grand Canyon nearly a billion years before the Colorado River carved it. The ancient landscape could also help explain why enormous sections of North America’s geological record appear to be missing.

mix_items.title: “One-in-a-million” sea creature fossil preserves soft tissue for 450 million years
mix_items.summary: Scientists have identified exceptionally rare soft tissue preserved in a 450-million-year-old crinoid fossil, more than 200 million years older than the first dinosaurs. Its delicate tube feet offer a remarkable new window into how some of Earth’s earliest reef animals lived, fed, and evolved.

mix_items.title: A new Ice Age species was hiding in la brea tar pits fossils for decades
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered a new extinct amphibian species hiding in the fossil collections of Los Angeles’ La Brea Tar Pits. Named Spea labreae, the Ice Age spadefoot toad is an exceptionally rare find—only one other extinct Pleistocene amphibian has ever been identified in North America. Its bones had been sitting in collections since the 1950s before a researcher noticed features that set it apart from known species.
